group.passage: Today a text message can cross the Atlantic Ocean in less than a second. For most of history, however, news could travel no faster than the ship that carried it. The table shows how the time needed to send word between Europe and North America shrank over nearly a century and a half. In 1818, a company began sending sailing ships between New York and Liverpool on fixed dates, so people could finally plan their trips with some certainty. These ships were built to be safe rather than fast, and a crossing of under three weeks was considered a good one. Steam power cut the trip further, and by 1850 the fastest steamships needed less than eleven days. The real breakthrough was expected to come from a wire laid along the ocean floor. After several failed attempts, a telegraph cable finally linked the two continents in August 1858. Yet the line was painfully slow: a 98-word greeting from Queen Victoria to the American president took 17 hours to get through. Hoping to push the weak signals along faster, the engineer in charge raised the power to 2,000 volts. This turned out to be a serious mistake. Within about a month of opening, the cable fell silent when its covering burned through near Ireland. War and another broken cable in 1865 delayed success until 1866. This time the cable was carried by the Great Eastern, a giant ship that had failed as a passenger liner because it burned too much fuel. The new cable was twice as thick and worked at low voltage, and it could carry six to eight words a minute. News that had once needed about twelve days now crossed the ocean in minutes. Later inventions removed the need for wires. In 1903, messages between President Theodore Roosevelt and Britain’s King Edward VII crossed by radio, though the station could send messages only late at night, when conditions were best. In 1962, the satellite Telstar carried live television pictures across the Atlantic for the first time, but only for about 18 minutes each time it passed overhead. Still, the ocean floor has not lost its role: today, cables lying there carry about 98 percent of the world’s information.

option_notes_zh.A: 女王的問候是前面舉的例子，用來說明電纜很慢；問候本身不是錯誤。

option_notes_zh.D: 最後一句說今天約 98% 的資訊是靠海底電纜傳送，不是衛星。

這兩個限制有什麼共同點？

translation_zh.text:
今天，一則簡訊不到一秒就能越過大西洋。然而在歷史上大部分的時間裡，消息傳得再快，也快不過載著它的那艘船。表格顯示，在將近一個半世紀裡，從歐洲到北美洲傳送消息所需的時間如何縮短。

1818 年，一家公司開始在固定日期派帆船往返紐約與利物浦，人們終於能比較有把握地安排行程。這些船造得重安全而不重速度，三個星期以內的航程就算順利。蒸汽動力讓航程進一步縮短，到了 1850 年，最快的蒸汽船只要不到十一天。

真正的突破，人們寄望於沿著海底鋪設的一條電線。經過幾次失敗之後，一條電報電纜終於在 1858 年 8 月連接了兩塊大陸。然而這條線路慢得令人難受：維多利亞女王給美國總統的一則 98 個字的問候，花了 17 個小時才傳完。負責的工程師希望讓微弱的訊號跑得快一點，把電力提高到 2,000 伏特。這後來證明是個嚴重的錯誤。啟用大約一個月內，電纜的外層就在愛爾蘭附近燒穿，從此沉寂。

戰爭，加上 1865 年又一次電纜斷裂，讓成功延到 1866 年才到來。這一次，電纜由 Great Eastern 號運送；這艘巨輪當客輪失敗，因為太耗燃料。新電纜粗了一倍、在低電壓下運作，每分鐘可以傳六到八個字。過去要大約十二天才能送到的消息，現在幾分鐘就越過了大洋。

後來的發明讓電線不再必要。1903 年，美國總統老羅斯福與英國國王愛德華七世之間的訊息透過無線電越洋傳送，不過電台只能在深夜、條件最好的時候發送。1962 年，Telstar 衛星第一次把電視直播畫面送過大西洋，但它每次經過上空只能傳送大約 18 分鐘。儘管如此，海底並沒有失去它的角色：今天，躺在那裡的電纜承載了全世界約 98% 的資訊。

【表 1】越洋傳訊，1818–1962：1818 年帆船定期班，18–20 天（紐約—利物浦第一條定期航線上順利的航程）；1838 年蒸汽船 Great Western，15 天（英國到紐約）；1850 年蒸汽船 Atlantic，10 天 16 小時（紐約到利物浦）；1858 年第一條電報電纜，98 個字要 17 小時（約一個月後停止運作）；1866 年第二條電報電纜，每分鐘 6–8 個字（由 Great Eastern 號鋪設）；1903 年無線電報，每分鐘約 17 個字（每字 50 美分；晚上 10 點到凌晨 2 點發送）；1962 年 Telstar 衛星，電視直播畫面（每次經過約 18 分鐘）。

open_tasks.prompt: The passage describes several ways of sending news across the Atlantic. Which change do you think made the biggest difference to people’s lives, and why? Answer in one or two English sentences.
reference_answers: The 1866 cable made the biggest difference, because news that had taken about twelve days by ship could arrive in minutes.
I think the satellite mattered most, because people could finally watch events on the other side of the ocean as they happened.
